parts.note: surface reading: a fee or price too steep to defend
setter's reading: an allegation of wrongdoing that is untrue

explanation.surface: An overcharged bill that the seller cannot defend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests money, but it is the legal sense: an accusation, here one that is false.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal charge is an allegation, and one with no grounds in truth is a false accusation.

parts.note: surface reading: a soldier who carries the regiment's colours
setter's reading: the pole that holds up a flag, a standard being a flag

explanation.walkthrough: A standard-bearer is normally a person; here it is the pole on which the standard is flown.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a banner, and the upright pole that carries one is a flagstaff.

parts.note: surface reading: a smart overcoat worn on top of other clothes
setter's reading: a glossy final layer of varnish on furniture

explanation.walkthrough: 'Topcoat' sounds like clothing, but it is the last coat of finish brushed onto wood.
explanation.definitionFit: This hard glossy varnish is applied as the final finishing layer over wood or metal.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the verb, to pick by vote
second meaning: the adjective, as in a president who has won but not yet taken office

explanation.walkthrough: The same word serves as verb and as adjective placed after a noun, as in 'bride-elect'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick by voting is to elect, and someone picked but not yet installed is described as elect.

clue.text: Weep before taking part in the vault

indicators.note: before says the first piece is placed ahead of the second in the grid

parts.note: to weep is to cry
PT is the standard abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: Someone sheds tears before playing their role inside a burial chamber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking part' reads as one phrase about joining in, but only 'part' supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A crypt is an underground vaulted chamber beneath a church, often used for burial.

parts.note: surface reading: the idiom for something wonderful
setter's reading: literally not belonging to the planet, so ghostly or alien

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means 'superb', but the question mark invites a literal reading: not of the Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something supernatural or alien does not belong to our planet, which is the literal sense of the answer.

clue.text: Nothing appearing in two different parts of manuals rewritten that's deviating from the norm

indicators.text: appearing in two different parts of
indicators.note: the nothing symbol shows up twice, at two separate places inside the other word
a rewritten text has its letters set out afresh, so the word manuals is rearranged

parts.note: nothing is zero, written as the letter O; 'two different parts' calls for it twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sentence about a word that pops up oddly in two places in rewritten handbooks.
explanation.walkthrough: Two O's go into the rearranged MANUALS at different points: AN-O-MAL-O-US.
explanation.definitionFit: Something anomalous departs from what is normal or expected, an irregular exception.

parts.note: surface reading: a question about putting blooms from Japan in order
setter's reading: the formal name of the Japanese art of floral arrangement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranging' looks like an anagram signal, but no letters are moved: the whole clue describes a traditional art.
explanation.definitionFit: Ikebana is the traditional Japanese art of composing cut flowers and branches.

parts.note: setter's reading: a reckless trapeze artist performs with no safety net below
surface reading: a musical work, here one written for nine players

explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as NO NET, what a reckless acrobat works without, and is also a piece for nine performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a musical piece scored for nine instruments or voices.

indicators.note: a mangled object has been crushed out of shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A prototype car's budget tyre has been chewed up.
explanation.definitionFit: An archetype is the first pattern or prototype from which later copies are made.

clue.text: Love this in Biarritz, an area of water

parts.note: love is a score of zero in tennis, written O
ce is French for this; Biarritz is a French seaside town
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone adores this spot in the French resort, a stretch of sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Biarritz signals a French word: 'this' becomes CE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocean is a vast expanse of salt water, such as the Atlantic beside Biarritz.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stocky, short and thickset
second meaning: to crouch low on the heels

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a brief rest, but the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stocky figure is described as squat, and crouching on the heels is to squat.

clue.text: Call commander not heartlessly a virago

indicators.note: without a heart, the middle letter of the word not is removed

parts.note: to call something is to term it
an aga is a Turkish military commander
taken as written before the deletion

explanation.surface: An officer is ruthlessly labelled a shrew.
explanation.walkthrough: NOT loses its middle letter to leave NT.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is an overbearing, bad-tempered woman, the same thing as a virago.

indicators.note: about means around, so the two articles sit on either side of the word for refuse

parts.note: two indefinite articles, a and a
an ort is a scrap of leftover food, i.e. refuse

explanation.surface: An instruction to turn down items about the body's chief blood vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun: rubbish, an ORT.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorta is the largest artery, carrying blood out from the heart.

clue.text: Pat's into a different hors d'oeuvre

indicators.note: different means changed in form, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pat has taken up an unusual starter.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the Italian name for a starter of cold meats and vegetables served before the meal.

parts.note: surface reading: a call that it is time someone got educated
setter's reading: the age at which a child begins attending classes

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an exhortation, but describes the stage of childhood when lessons begin.
explanation.definitionFit: The point in childhood when a pupil must begin formal classes is this phrase.

clue.text: Friends on the way up remain with comedy

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the word for friends from bottom to top

parts.note: pals are friends
to stick is to stay put

explanation.surface: Pals whose careers are rising stay with comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapstick is boisterous physical comedy, named after a clown's paddle.

clue.text: Lee's moved to unknown place that's neither here nor there

indicators.note: things that are moved are shifted about, so these letters change places

parts.note: taken as written
where asks after an unknown location

explanation.surface: Lee has relocated to somewhere unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neither here nor there' usually means irrelevant; read literally it is a place other than this one.
explanation.definitionFit: Somewhere other than here or there is literally in another place.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the title of a US president's spouse
second meaning: in Genesis, the earliest woman created

explanation.walkthrough: Eve, as the original woman in the Bible, is the earliest female literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The spouse of a head of state is given this title, and Eve was the original woman in Genesis.

clue.text: Strange brick-carrier I included made of a hard metal

indicators.note: included means taken inside, so the carrier and the letter go within the word for strange

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange
a hod is a builder's trough for carrying bricks
taken as written

explanation.surface: An odd labourer joined the team, a tough metal type.
explanation.walkthrough: The page's stray bar is the letter I. Rum is old British slang for peculiar, and a hod is the trough a bricklayer's mate carries on the shoulder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodium is a hard, silvery-white metallic element of the platinum group.

indicators.note: sails that are trimmed are adjusted and reset, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailing friend of Paul's has cut back the canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trimmed' tempts a deletion, but all five letters are kept and reordered. Paul is the apostle.
explanation.definitionFit: In Acts, Silas travelled as the apostle Paul's missionary companion.

indicators.note: surrounding means wrapped around, so the word for fat goes outside the other piece

parts.note: lard is pig fat
any can mean some, as in 'have you any?'

explanation.surface: A bit of grease is wrapped round a piece of string.
explanation.definitionFit: A lanyard is a cord worn round the neck or used on ships to secure things.

clue.text: This candidate cannot fail to get a seat

definitions.text: This candidate cannot fail to get a seat

parts.note: surface reading: someone sure to find a chair

parts.words: This candidate cannot fail to get a seat
parts.note: setter's reading: an election contender with no rival is returned to parliament automatically

explanation.walkthrough: A seat here is a parliamentary constituency; a candidate standing alone wins it without a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate facing no rival in an election is returned with no contest at all.

indicators.note: of means taken from, so the letters are drawn out of the following words

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the way a brute named Richard speaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugric is a branch of the Finno-Ugric languages, including Hungarian.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: do. is the written abbreviation of this word
second meaning: the same again, the thing just mentioned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a verb, as in 'do as you are told', but it is the abbreviation 'do.' used in lists.
explanation.definitionFit: Written 'do.' in lists, the word means the same as stated before.

clue.text: Is returning with previously unknown strength

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is is read right to left

parts.note: taken as written
something new was not known before

explanation.surface: Someone comes back with fresh vigour.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinew means a tendon, and by extension physical muscle power.

indicators.note: a tattered thing is torn to pieces, so the letters are scattered and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The ragged canvas of a ship's sail and its threads.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff plant fibre from an agave, used for rope and matting.

clue.text: Hurries round one old castle perhaps

indicators.note: round means encircling, so the word for hurries is wrapped about the other piece

parts.note: to hurry is to run
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone dashes about an ancient fortress.
explanation.definitionFit: An old castle is an example of crumbling remains, hence the 'perhaps'.

parts.note: surface reading: someone who left unwillingly, lacking determination
setter's reading: died leaving no legal testament

explanation.walkthrough: 'Departed' is a euphemism for died, and 'will' is the legal document, not willpower.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who dies leaving no valid legal testament is said to die in this state.

parts.note: setter's reading: Clapham Common is a large park in south London
surface reading: facts familiar to all who live there

explanation.walkthrough: Clapham Common is a London park, so its local lore is literally Common lore; the phrase means facts known to everybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Facts that are widely known by the general public are described with this phrase.
